title: not a building
hook: not a building — the people; the Greek word means "the called-out ones"
tomorrow: the shortest gospel, the mountain ahead

segments.voice: Yesterday, communion. A table, bread, a cup, and the words: remember me. Your line: a meal is a memory. Did you eat one meal slowly? Day twenty.

Say the word church and a picture comes up. A steeple. Stained glass. Maybe a cathedral so big your voice echoes, maybe a strip-mall storefront with folding chairs. Everybody pictures a building. But here's a fact that surprises people. For about the first two hundred years, Christians had almost no church buildings at all. They met in kitchens and courtyards. In somebody's living room, around somebody's table. Paul ends one of his letters sending greetings to a married couple, and in the old King James he adds: "greet the church that is in their house." The church was in the house. Which means it wasn't the house. Today's word is what it was.
screen: `SAY "CHURCH." WHAT DO YOU SEE?` → `200 YEARS, ALMOST NO BUILDINGS.` → `"THE CHURCH THAT IS IN THEIR HOUSE."`

segments.voice: The church. The word in the New Testament is Greek: ekklesia. It's made of two small pieces. Ek, out. And a word for calling. The called-out ones. In a Greek city, the ekklesia was the assembly: the citizens called out of their homes to gather and decide things together. It wasn't a place. It was people, showing up. So when the first Christians needed a word for themselves, that's the one they picked. Not the temple. Not a sacred site. The gathering. Paul pushes it further. He tells one of his churches: "ye are the body of Christ." Hands, feet, eyes, ears. All different. None of them the whole thing, and none of them able to say to the others, I don't need you. That's how he pictures a church: not a crowd of the same person, but a body of very different ones. And then there's the promise Jesus makes in Matthew's Gospel, the smallest possible church. "For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them." Two or three. Not two or three hundred. Christians today gather in every size and shape there is. Some in cathedrals that took centuries to build. Some in house churches, still meeting around a kitchen table the old way. Some in a hospital room, or a prison, or on a video call. Churches differ a lot about how they're led and how they're joined. But almost every one of them would say this much: the building is where the church meets. The people are the church.
screen: `EKKLESIA — THE CALLED-OUT ONES.` · `AN ASSEMBLY, NOT A PLACE.` · `"YE ARE THE BODY OF CHRIST."` · `TWO OR THREE.` · then, large: `THE PEOPLE ARE THE CHURCH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Seventy-five seconds. Sit, and breathe out slowly. Now think of the two or three people you'd call if something went wrong tonight. The ones who'd show up. Picture them, one at a time. Where they live. Their faces. And then widen it a little: someone who showed up for you once and never knew what it meant. If you pray, you can gather them in your prayer, the way Christians gather in his name. If you don't, just let them be gathered here with you for a minute. The bell holds the time.
The church. Ekklesia. Not a building: the called-out ones, gathered. Twentieth word.
Your line: find two or three. Today, gather with two or three people on purpose. A coffee, a call, a walk. Tell them why you wanted to. Day twenty.

screen: `DAY 20 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE SHORTEST GOSPEL, THE MOUNTAIN AHEAD.`

howItsDone: Most Christians gather with a church on Sundays for worship, and many also meet in small groups at home during the week. Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant churches are organized differently, but all speak of the church as the people, not the building.

fork.setup: you're one of the first Christians, about the year 60. it's the Lord's day. where do you go to meet the church?
options: a believer's house, around their table.
fork.reveal: a house. there were almost no church buildings yet. the church met in homes, and Paul greeted "the church that is in their house."

original.note: Greek. ek (out) + a word for calling: the assembly, the called-out ones. the New Testament's word for church.

trapdoor: what you thought: a building with a steeple.
what it means: the people, gathered. ekklesia, the called-out ones. the building is only where they meet.
what a scholar hears: ekklesia was the Greek city's assembly of citizens. early churches met in homes; one house church found at Dura-Europos in Syria dates from the third century.

notes: 'The called-out ones' follows the index; many scholars note that in ordinary Greek ekklesia simply meant 'assembly' and the etymology (ek + kaleo) was not felt strongly. The teach gives both (called-out ones, and the city assembly). Please confirm.
'About the first two hundred years, almost no church buildings' is the common historical summary (the Dura-Europos house church, c. AD 230s–240s, is among the earliest known); confirm wording.
Romans 16:5 quote begins 'Likewise greet the church that is in their house' in the KJV; the script quotes from 'greet'. Similar greetings: 1 Corinthians 16:19, Colossians 4:15, Philemon 2.
Fork dates the scene 'about the year 60'; Paul's Romans is usually dated c. AD 57. Approximate on purpose.
Not included: the English word 'church' is often traced to Greek kyriakon, 'the Lord's (house)'. Could be added at a Keeper's discretion.
